children: By Reporting and photography by Sune Engel Rasmussen
BLANDFORD FORUM, England — The pub is a pillar of British culture as iconic as fish and chips, afternoon tea and the monarchy.
And it is in deep crisis.

Rising utility bills, high taxes and sober-curious Gen Z'ers are undermining the centuries-old business model of providing a drink and cheap bite to eat. To survive, pubs across Britain are exploring some of the more niche needs of their communities to build revenue beyond pies and pints.

The Ivy House in south London hosts a regular feminist sci-fi book club, a knitting circle and musical theater classes for children. In Cornwall, the Star Inn offers menopause fitness and is opening a unisex hair salon on site.
On a recent evening, south London's Old Nun's Head, housed in a century-old Tudor-style building, crackled with energy as dozens of patrons gathered for a boisterous queer speed-dating event.
"A lot of pubs are stuck in an idea of what a traditional pub should be," said Allie Twist, the pub's 36-year-old manager. "Selling food and drink doesn't really cut it."

One in four pubs have closed in Britain since 2000, leaving around 44,000 still in business, the lowest on record. Nearly two shut each day in the first quarter of this year, up 26% from 2025, according to the British Beer and Pub Association. Nearly a quarter of those that survive are losing money.

There is more at stake than just boozers. Pubs are gathering places for people to compete in trivia nights, watch soccer games on television or just shoot the breeze with neighbors they might disagree with, often with their dog in tow.

It is a particular problem in rural areas, where pubs, or public houses, often take on several functions. Some serve as drop-in health clinics. The Anglers Rest, a 17th-century coaching inn in Bamford near Sheffield, doubles as a post office and polling station.

Nick Moores, who last year moved 200 miles from Manchester to take on the derelict Butchers Arms in West Somerset, says pubs are often the only place where women can socialize safely out in the middle of nowhere. "They would normally go home, close the curtains and not see anyone until 10 in the morning," he said.
To keep customers coming, his pub holds ancient wassailing rituals, where hundreds of patrons fire shotguns and throw stones into orchards to ward off evil spirits.

Politicians make a point of pouring pints on the campaign trail in the hope of winning a few votes. Prime Minister Andy Burnham offered more support when he took office earlier this year. "Pubs need to know the cavalry is coming," he said, later announcing a 20% cut in business rates, worth about 1,100 pounds a year for each pub, or roughly $1,500.

Yet that is short of the GBP12,900 an average pub will pay in extra rates over the next three years, says trade association UKHospitality. And the U.K.'s 20% sales tax on hospitality is double that of France, Italy and Spain.
Another obstacle is cultural.

For all their beer-chugging reputation, Britons drink less of the stuff than they used to, partly because of changing alcohol habits among the young. U.K. per capita beer consumption has halved since 1980, from 17 pints a month to nine, according to consumer organization Campaign for Real Ale, or Camra, and more than half of it is drunk at home. In 1980, Britons mostly drank in the pub.

In 2021, villagers in Stoke Ferry in Norfolk fended off developers who had purchased the parish's last pub, the Blue Bell. Some 400 people bought shares to acquire the gutted building for GBP180,000. To remain inclusive the pub keeps a pint of ale at GBP4.80, equivalent to $6.35.
"There's no money in it," said Joanne Collins, who is part of the management.
A growing number of pubs have concluded that they need to give more reasons for people to go out to drink.

"The pub needs to be individual, it needs to be quirky, it needs to be different from the home you just left behind," said John Longden, founder of Pub is the Hub, a nonprofit advising pubs on how to serve community needs and combat loneliness. Pubs respond with garden allotments, micro libraries and, in remote locations, selling groceries.

Even larger chains of pubs are rethinking their approach. The family-owned Hall and Woodhouse has brewed beer for as long as the U.S. has existed as a country. But pints are no longer the profit driver. Coffee, tea and food account for more than half the revenue in the 45 pubs the brewery operates.

The business, founded in 1777 in Dorset in southwest England, is propped up by brewing and selling its own beer, and by renting an additional roughly 100 pubs to tenants. It also offers vacation accommodation. Still, it has closed nearly half of the 260 pubs it owned in 2000.

"There are now fewer, bigger pubs. That's the only way that you can make it work," said Anthony Woodhouse, chairperson of Hall and Woodhouse, and seventh-generation heir. "For the smaller, more super-local pub, the math just simply doesn't add up."

Back at the Old Nun's Head in south London, Twist said "public houses have a duty of care to the community." Hers is the local LGBTQ community, though the pub appears to count as many straight people among its regulars. She realized the potential two years ago, when she invited a queer pub from New York to co-host an event.
"We had about 500 lesbians come to the pub. That was a turning point," Twist said. "I just went all gay guns blazing after that."
Nazmia Jamal, an academic who recently organized a monthly reading group there called Lesbians Talk Issues, said no other venue in the area would have hosted the event.

"On the face of it, someone like me who is presenting like a Muslim lesbian is not the kind of person who is going to make a lot of money for your pub," she said. "But there was a generosity about it, like, we've got a space, and it should be for the community."
